stem: Of 60 employees at a company, 15 carpool to work and 20 arrive early. Six employees both carpool and arrive early. What is P(arrives early | carpools)?

rationales.A: Given that the employee carpools, the denominator is the 15 carpoolers; 6 of them arrive early, so 6/15 = 0.40.
rationales.B: The 9 is the number of carpoolers who do NOT arrive early (15 − 6); the denominator should be all 15 carpoolers.
rationales.C: This divides by the number who arrive early, which is P(carpools | arrives early), the reversed conditional.
rationales.D: This divides by all employees, giving the joint probability P(carpools and arrives early) rather than a conditional probability.

stem: In a school of 120 students, 48 are in band and 30 are in orchestra. Eighteen students are in both. What is P(in orchestra | in band)?

rationales.A: Given the student is in band, the sample space is the 48 band members; 18 of them are in orchestra, so 18/48 = 0.375.
rationales.B: This is the unconditional probability P(orchestra); knowing the student is in band changes the probability.
rationales.C: This uses orchestra members as the denominator, which is P(band | orchestra), the reversed conditional.
rationales.D: This is the joint probability P(band and orchestra), using the whole school as the denominator.

stem:
A store surveyed 200 customers and recorded age group and whether they bought online. The results are below.
Under 30, bought online: 50
Under 30, did not buy online: 30
30 or older, bought online: 40
30 or older, did not buy online: 80
What is P(under 30 | bought online)?

rationales.A: This divides by the 80 under-30 customers, which is P(bought online | under 30), the reversed conditional.
rationales.B: 90/200 = 0.45 is the marginal probability of buying online. The question asks what fraction of online buyers are under 30, so the numerator must be the 50 under-30 online buyers, not all 90 buyers.
rationales.C: This divides by all 200 customers, giving the joint probability instead of the conditional probability.
rationales.D: Among the 50 + 40 = 90 customers who bought online, 50 are under 30, so P = 50/90 ≈ 0.56.

stem: The probability that a randomly selected bulb from a production line is defective is 0.08. What is the probability that the bulb is not defective?

rationales.A: This subtracts in the wrong order (0.08 − 1); a probability cannot be negative, and the complement is 1 − 0.08 = 0.92.
rationales.B: The complement rule gives P(not defective) = 1 − 0.08 = 0.92.
rationales.C: This comes from treating 0.08 as 0.8 and computing 1 − 0.8; the complement of 0.08 is 0.92.
rationales.D: This repeats the probability of a defective bulb rather than its complement.

stem: The probability that a certain flight arrives on time is 0.82. What is the probability that the flight does not arrive on time?

rationales.A: By the complement rule, 1 − 0.82 = 0.18.
rationales.B: This subtracts 0.82 from 0.90 instead of from 1.
rationales.C: This is the probability of arriving on time, not its complement.
rationales.D: This adds 0.82 to 1; a probability cannot exceed 1, and the complement is 1 − 0.82.

stem: A forecaster says there is a 40% chance of snow tomorrow. What is the probability that it does not snow?

rationales.A: Writing 40% as 0.40, the complement is 1 − 0.40 = 0.60.
rationales.B: This converts 40% to 0.04 and then computes 1 − 0.04; 40% is 0.40, so the complement is 0.60.
rationales.C: This repeats the probability of snow instead of finding its complement.
rationales.D: This assumes snow and no snow are equally likely, which ignores the given 40% chance.

stem: At a school, the probability that a randomly selected student takes Spanish is 0.45, the probability the student takes music is 0.30, and the probability the student takes both is 0.10. What is the probability that a randomly selected student takes Spanish or music (or both)?

rationales.A: By the addition rule, P(Spanish or music) = 0.45 + 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.65.
rationales.B: This subtracts the overlap twice: 0.45 + 0.30 − 2(0.10) = 0.55.
rationales.C: This multiplies 0.45 × 0.30, which would be the probability of both only if the events were independent, and it is not the union.
rationales.D: This adds 0.45 and 0.30 without subtracting the overlap, so students taking both are counted twice.

stem: For two events A and B, P(A) = 0.70, P(B) = 0.40, and P(A and B) = 0.35. What is P(A or B)?

rationales.A: Using the addition rule, 0.70 + 0.40 − 0.35 = 0.75.
rationales.B: This is only P(A and B), the intersection.
rationales.C: This is 0.70 × 0.40, the probability of both under independence, not the probability of either.
rationales.D: This adds the two probabilities without subtracting the overlap; a probability cannot exceed 1.

stem: Among 80 students surveyed, 50 own a laptop, 30 own a tablet, and 15 own both. What is the probability that a randomly selected student from this group owns a laptop or a tablet?

rationales.A: This adds 50 and 30 without subtracting the 15 who own both, which would imply every student owns at least one device.
rationales.B: This multiplies the individual probabilities, which would be the probability of both under independence, not the union.
rationales.C: This is only the probability of owning both, the intersection.
rationales.D: The number owning at least one is 50 + 30 − 15 = 65, so the probability is 65/80 = 0.8125.

stem: A new thermometer is tested thousands of times on liquids with known temperatures. Its readings are tightly clustered, but they average 2.3 degrees above the true temperature no matter how many readings are averaged. What is the main problem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The estimator has high variability, since its readings are not equal to the true temperature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The readings are not independent, since each is above the true temperature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sample sizes are too small, since averaging more readings would remove the error.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The estimator is biased, since its readings are centered above the true value.

rationales.A: Variability is the spread of readings; the stem says they are tightly clustered, so the problem is the off-center location, not scatter.
rationales.B: Dependence between readings is not described; a consistent upward shift is a systematic error in the estimator, which is bias.
rationales.C: The stem says the error remains no matter how many readings are averaged; more data cannot fix a systematic offset.
rationales.D: An estimator whose values are systematically off target in one direction, even in the long run, is biased; here the center is about 2.3 degrees too high.

stem: In repeated random samples of size 100 from a population with true mean 50, a new estimator has a sampling distribution centered at 56 with a standard deviation of 1.5. Which statement best describes this estimator?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is unbiased with low variability, because its standard deviation is small.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is biased with high variability, since its values are far from 50.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is unbiased but has high variability, since it often misses 50.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is biased but has low variability: its values cluster near 56 instead of 50.

rationales.A: A small standard deviation shows low variability only; unbiasedness requires the center to equal 50, and this one is centered at 56.
rationales.B: Being far from 50 is explained by the bias of about 6 units; the standard deviation of 1.5 shows the values are not widely scattered.
rationales.C: It misses 50 because its center is 56, which is bias; and a standard deviation of 1.5 is small, not large.
rationales.D: The center of the sampling distribution, 56, is not the true value of 50, so it is biased; a standard deviation of 1.5 shows its values are tightly clustered.

stem: A statistician simulates 2,000 random samples to estimate a true proportion of 0.40. The 2,000 sample proportions average exactly 0.40, but individual values range from 0.25 to 0.55. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The estimator is unbiased but has high variability: its average is 0.40, yet single estimates are widely spread.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The estimator is unbiased, so increasing the sample size cannot reduce how widely the estimates vary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The estimator is biased, because many individual estimates differ from the true proportion of 0.40.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The estimator is unbiased with low variability, because its average equals 0.40.

rationales.A: The sampling distribution is centered at the true value of 0.40, so there is no bias, but the wide range from 0.25 to 0.55 shows high variability.
rationales.B: Increasing the sample size reduces the standard error, so larger samples would make the estimates cluster more tightly around 0.40.
rationales.C: Bias refers to the center of the sampling distribution, which is exactly 0.40; individual estimates differing from 0.40 reflects variability.
rationales.D: The average only shows the center; the estimates range from 0.25 to 0.55, which is a wide spread, so variability is high.

stem: In a random sample of 250 adults, 105 say they use public transit weekly. A researcher wants to know whether the proportion of all adults who use public transit weekly is less than 0.45. Which hypotheses should be tested?

rationales.A: The claim is that the population proportion is less than 0.45, so the null sets p equal to 0.45 and the alternative is left-tailed.
rationales.B: Hypotheses are about the population parameter p, not the sample statistic p̂.
rationales.C: This is right-tailed, but the question asks whether the proportion is less than 0.45.
rationales.D: Hypotheses use the claimed value, not the sample proportion 105/250 = 0.42.

stem: A manufacturer says 10% of its chips are defective. In a random sample of 300 chips, 45 are defective. A quality inspector wants to know whether the true defect rate differs from 10%. Which hypotheses are correct?

rationales.A: 0.15 is the sample proportion 45/300; hypotheses use the claimed parameter value of 0.10.
rationales.B: Although the sample proportion is above 0.10, the question asks about a difference in either direction, so a one-sided alternative does not match.
rationales.C: The question asks whether the rate differs from 10% in either direction, so the null is p = 0.10 and the alternative is two-sided.
rationales.D: The null and alternative are reversed; the null must contain the equality.

stem: A candidate needs more than 40% of voters to win. In a random sample of 80 voters, 38 support the candidate. The campaign wants to test whether the proportion of all voters supporting the candidate exceeds 40%. Which hypotheses are correct?

rationales.A: The claim is that support exceeds 40%, so the alternative is right-tailed and the null sets p equal to 0.40.
rationales.B: The alternative should describe a range, here p > 0.40, not a single value taken from the sample.
rationales.C: Hypotheses concern the population parameter p and its claimed value of 0.40, not the sample proportion 38/80 = 0.475.
rationales.D: This tests the opposite direction; the campaign wants evidence that support is greater than 0.40.

stem: A basketball player makes each free throw independently with probability 0.3. Let X be the number of free throws made in 4 attempts. What is P(X = 0)?

rationales.A: This is the probability of missing a single shot, not of missing all 4.
rationales.B: X is binomial with n = 4 and p = 0.3, so P(X = 0) = (0.7)^4 = 0.2401.
rationales.C: This is (0.3)^4, the probability that all 4 shots are made, using p instead of 1 − p.
rationales.D: This is P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.2401, the probability of at least one made shot.

stem: Each seed in a packet of 6 sprouts independently with probability 0.2. Let X be the number of seeds that sprout. What is P(X = 0)?

rationales.A: X is binomial with n = 6 and p = 0.2, so P(X = 0) = (0.8)^6 ≈ 0.2621.
rationales.B: This is P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.2621, the probability that at least one seed sprouts.
rationales.C: This is the probability a single seed fails to sprout, not that all 6 fail.
rationales.D: This is (0.2)^6 ≈ 0.000064, the probability that all 6 sprout, using p instead of 1 − p.

stem: A pollster makes 8 independent phone calls. Each call is answered with probability 0.35. Let X be the number of calls that are answered. What is P(X = 0)?

rationales.A: X is binomial with n = 8 and p = 0.35, so P(X = 0) = (0.65)^8 ≈ 0.0319.
rationales.B: This is the probability that one call is unanswered, not that all 8 are.
rationales.C: This is (0.35)^8 ≈ 0.000225, the probability all 8 calls are answered, using p instead of 1 − p.
rationales.D: This is P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − 0.0319, the probability that at least one call is answered.

stem: Two researchers test the same hypotheses and the same true parameter value. Study X uses α = 0.10 with n = 400. Study Y uses α = 0.01 with n = 100. Which statement about their power is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The studies have equal power, because they test the same hypotheses with the same true parameter value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Study Y has lower power, because both its smaller α and smaller sample size reduce power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Study X has lower power, because the larger α makes a Type I error more likely, which reduces power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Study X has lower power, because a larger sample size increases variability and so makes rejection less likely.

rationales.A: Power depends on n and α as well as the true value, and these two differ in both (400 vs 100, 0.10 vs 0.01).
rationales.B: A smaller α makes rejecting H₀ harder, and a smaller n gives a larger standard error; both lower the chance of detecting a false null, so Y has lower power.
rationales.C: A larger α increases the chance of rejecting H₀, which raises power; it does not reduce it.
rationales.D: A larger sample size decreases the standard error, which increases power.

stem: A test of H₀: p = 0.50 versus Hₐ: p > 0.50 uses n = 100 and α = 0.05, and the true proportion is p = 0.60. Which change would increase the power of the test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increasing the sample size to 400, which reduces the standard error.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreasing the sample size to 25, since a smaller sample has fewer chances for error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lowering α to 0.01, which makes the test more careful about rejecting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Using the hypothesized value 0.58 in place of 0.50, so the null is closer to the truth.

rationales.A: A larger n shrinks the standard error of p̂, making a true difference easier to detect, so power increases.
rationales.B: A smaller sample gives a larger standard error, which lowers power; sample size reduction does not reduce error.
rationales.C: A smaller α makes rejection harder, which reduces the probability of rejecting a false H₀ and so decreases power.
rationales.D: A smaller gap between the null value and the true value makes the difference harder to detect, which lowers power.

stem: A significance test with α = 0.05 has a Type II error probability of 0.35 when the true proportion is 0.60. What is the power of the test against that alternative?

rationales.A: This multiplies α by the Type II probability (0.05 × 0.35); power is found by subtraction, not multiplication.
rationales.B: This is 1 − α = 0.95, which is the probability of not making a Type I error when H₀ is true, not power.
rationales.C: This is the probability of a Type II error itself; power is its complement.
rationales.D: Power is the probability of rejecting a false null, 1 − P(Type II error) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

stem: A medical team tests whether a new drug lowers systolic blood pressure more than a placebo. They enroll 36 patients, 18 men and 18 women, and randomly assign drug or placebo separately within the men and within the women, instead of randomizing all 36 patients together. What is the main statistical advantage of assigning treatments within each sex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It lets the team conclude the drug works for all adults, since both sexes were included in the trial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It makes the placebo group unnecessary, because sex differences are already accounted for.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It eliminates confounding from every lurking variable, including ones the team never measured.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It removes blood-pressure variation that is due to sex from the drug-versus-placebo comparison, making a real drug effect easier to detect.

rationales.A: Blocking does not extend conclusions to a population; generalizing depends on how the 36 patients were selected, not on how treatments were assigned.
rationales.B: A placebo or other comparison group is still needed to measure the drug effect; blocking adjusts only for sex differences.
rationales.C: Blocking only controls the blocked variable (sex); protection against unmeasured variables comes from random assignment, not from the blocks.
rationales.D: Sex is a known source of variability in the response. Comparing drug and placebo inside each sex block keeps that variation from blurring the treatment difference, which raises power.

stem: A teacher wants to compare a new study app with textbook review. She has 60 students: 30 in a morning section and 30 in an afternoon section. Within each section she randomly assigns half the students to the app and half to the textbook, rather than randomizing all 60 together. What is the primary benefit of this approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows the teacher to claim cause and effect, which complete randomization of all 60 students would not allow.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It guarantees the class period has no effect on test scores in either treatment group.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It makes the app and textbook groups larger, which gives more data for the comparison.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It accounts for score differences caused by class period, so differences between the two study methods stand out more clearly.

rationales.A: Random assignment, whether across all 60 students or within blocks, is what supports cause-and-effect conclusions; blocking is not required for that.
rationales.B: Blocking does not remove the effect of class period; it only prevents that effect from being mixed in with the treatment comparison.
rationales.C: Blocking splits the same 60 students into the same two treatment groups; it adds no students and does not enlarge either group.
rationales.D: Class period may affect scores. Randomizing within each section separates that effect from the app-versus-textbook comparison, reducing unexplained variability.

stem: A veterinary researcher compares two diets for weight loss in 24 dogs: 12 small-breed dogs and 12 large-breed dogs. Diet is randomly assigned separately within the small-breed group and within the large-breed group. Compared with randomly assigning diets to all 24 dogs at once, what does this design mainly accomplish?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It makes the dogs and owners unaware of which diet each dog receives, so expectations cannot affect results.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It raises the number of dogs in the study from 24 to 48, which strengthens the evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It removes the need for a second diet group because breed size is already being compared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It controls variation in weight loss that is related to breed size, so a real difference between the diets is easier to detect.

rationales.A: Hiding treatment assignments is blinding, which is a separate feature; grouping dogs by size does not conceal anything from anyone.
rationales.B: The same 24 dogs are used either way; splitting them into size groups does not increase the number of animals.
rationales.C: The two diets are still compared against each other; breed size is only used to organize the random assignment, not to replace a comparison.
rationales.D: Breed size is expected to influence weight loss. Randomizing within each size group keeps that source of variation from hiding the diet effect.

stem: A random sample of 600 teenagers in a school district is used to build a 90% confidence interval for the proportion of all teenagers in the district who own a laptop. The interval is (0.29, 0.35). Which statement is a correct interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 90% of teenagers in the district own a laptop, give or take 3 percentage points.

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is a 90% probability that a new random sample of 600 teenagers will have a sample proportion between 0.29 and 0.35.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Between 29% and 35% of the 600 sampled teenagers own a laptop, and we are 90% sure of this.

choices.label: D
choices.text: We are 90% confident that the interval from 0.29 to 0.35 captures the proportion of all teenagers in the district who own a laptop.

rationales.A: The interval estimates the single population proportion; it does not say that 90% of individuals have the characteristic.
rationales.B: The confidence level does not give the probability that a future sample proportion falls in this particular interval; it concerns the method capturing the population proportion.
rationales.C: The sample proportion is known exactly from the data (and lies in the middle of the interval); the interval estimates the population proportion, not the sample's.
rationales.D: The 90% describes how reliably the interval-building method captures the fixed population proportion over many random samples.

stem: A news site reports a 95% confidence interval of (0.53, 0.59) for the proportion of registered voters in a county who favor a school bond, using a random sample of 1,000 voters. Which statement correctly explains what the 95% confidence level means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 95% of the 1,000 voters in the sample favor the school bond, give or take a few points.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 95% of intervals built this way from repeated random samples would contain the true proportion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is a 5% chance that this sample proportion lies outside the interval from 0.53 to 0.59.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The probability is 0.95 that the true proportion of supporters in the county is exactly 0.56.

rationales.A: The confidence level is not a percentage of individuals; the sample proportion of supporters is near 0.56, not 0.95.
rationales.B: This describes the long-run capture rate of the interval-building method across repeated random samples, which is what the confidence level represents.
rationales.C: The sample proportion is the midpoint of the interval, so it always lies inside it; the 5% refers to intervals that miss the population value.
rationales.D: The true proportion is a single fixed value, and 0.56 is only the sample estimate at the interval's center; the chance of exact equality is not 0.95.

stem: A company surveys a random sample of 1,200 of its customers and computes a 99% confidence interval of (0.72, 0.78) for the proportion of all its customers who are satisfied. Which statement is a correct interpretation of this interval?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 99% of the 1,200 surveyed customers gave a satisfaction rating between 0.72 and 0.78.

choices.label: B
choices.text: We are 99% confident that the true proportion of all the company's customers who are satisfied is between 0.72 and 0.78.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is a 99% probability that the next customer surveyed will be satisfied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The true proportion of satisfied customers changes from sample to sample and falls between 0.72 and 0.78 in 99% of samples.

rationales.A: The interval gives plausible values for a population proportion; it does not describe how individual customers' ratings are distributed.
rationales.B: The 99% refers to the reliability of the method: about 99% of intervals constructed this way capture the true customer-satisfaction proportion.
rationales.C: The interval says nothing about 0.99 as a probability for one customer; the estimated proportion satisfied is about 0.75.
rationales.D: The population proportion is fixed; it is the interval that changes from sample to sample.

stem: A pediatrician tells a parent that a baby's weight is at the 20th percentile for babies of the same age. What does this mean?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This baby weighs 20% less than the average baby of the same age.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 20% of babies that age weigh more than this baby.

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 20% of babies that age weigh the same as or less than this baby.

choices.label: D
choices.text: This baby's weight is 20% of the way from the lightest to the heaviest baby.

rationales.A: Percentile reflects rank within the group, not a percent difference from the mean weight.
rationales.B: If about 20% weigh more, the baby would be near the 80th percentile; at the 20th percentile it is about 80% who weigh at or above this baby.
rationales.C: A percentile gives the percentage of values at or below the given value, so the 20th percentile has about 20% of babies at or below it.
rationales.D: Percentile counts the fraction of individuals at or below a value, not the position of the value within the range from minimum to maximum.

stem: A class of 40 students takes a quiz. Exactly 32 of the 40 scores, including Dana's, are less than or equal to Dana's score. Which percentile is Dana's score?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 80th percentile

choices.label: B
choices.text: 20th percentile

choices.label: C
choices.text: 8th percentile

choices.label: D
choices.text: 32nd percentile

rationales.A: Percentile = (number of scores at or below) / (total) x 100 = 32/40 x 100 = 80.
rationales.B: 8 scores are above Dana's, and 8/40 = 20%; that is the percentage above her, not at or below.
rationales.C: 8 is the number of scores above Dana's; using that count directly as the percentile is neither the percent at or below nor even a percent.
rationales.D: 32 is the count of scores at or below Dana's; it must be divided by 40 and converted to a percent.

stem: An employee at a large company learns that her salary is at the 60th percentile of all salaries at the company. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 60% of employees at the company earn her salary or less.

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 60% of employees at the company earn more than she does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her salary is 60% of the highest salary at the company.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She has the 60th highest salary among the employees at the company.

rationales.A: The 60th percentile means about 60% of the values are at or below that value.
rationales.B: That would put her near the 40th percentile; at the 60th percentile about 40% earn more.
rationales.C: Percentile compares the count of employees below, not her salary as a fraction of the maximum.
rationales.D: Percentile is a percentage of the group, not a rank; the 60th highest in a large company would be a much higher percentile.

stem: Researchers examine the medical records of 500 adults, noting whether each person takes a daily vitamin D supplement and whether the person had a bone fracture in the past five years. The researchers do not tell anyone to start or stop taking supplements. What type of study is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single-blind experiment

choices.label: B
choices.text: An observational study

choices.label: C
choices.text: A randomized block experiment

choices.label: D
choices.text: A completely randomized experiment

rationales.A: An experiment requires an imposed treatment, and nothing about blinding is described.
rationales.B: The researchers only record existing behavior and outcomes; no treatment is imposed on the adults.
rationales.C: There are no blocks and no random assignment of any treatment.
rationales.D: No one is randomly assigned to supplements; people chose for themselves.

stem: A teacher lets her 40 students choose either flashcards or practice tests as their study method for a unit, then compares the two groups' scores on the unit exam. What type of study is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A randomized block design, because the students form two groups.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A randomized experiment, because the teacher compared two study methods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An observational study, because students chose their own study method instead of being assigned one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A matched-pairs experiment, because every student took the same exam.

rationales.A: Blocks are formed before treatments are randomly assigned within them; here the groups came from student choice.
rationales.B: Comparing two groups is not enough; an experiment requires the researcher to assign treatments, ideally at random.
rationales.C: The teacher did not impose the treatment; students self-selected into the groups, so this is observational and cannot show cause and effect.
rationales.D: Matched pairs requires pairing subjects or measuring each subject twice under assigned conditions, which did not occur.

stem: Researchers randomly assign 90 volunteers to one of three diets and measure each volunteer's cholesterol level after eight weeks. What type of study is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An observational study, because cholesterol was only measured at the end.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A randomized experiment, because the researchers assigned the diets to the volunteers at random.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An observational study, because the volunteers were not a random sample of adults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A sample survey, because 90 people provided data.

rationales.A: Measuring a response does not make a study observational; what matters is that the researchers imposed the diets.
rationales.B: The researchers imposed the treatments (diets) and used random assignment, which defines a randomized experiment.
rationales.C: Volunteer subjects limit generalization, but the study type depends on whether treatments are imposed, and they were.
rationales.D: A sample survey gathers opinions or facts from a sample without imposing treatments; here diets were assigned.

stem: A school district wants to learn parents' opinions about school lunches. It mails questionnaires only to the families listed in the PTA directory. Which bias is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Voluntary response bias, because parents decide whether to fill out the form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Undercoverage bias, because parents not in the PTA directory have no chance to be selected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonresponse bias, because some mailed questionnaires will not be returned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No bias, because every questionnaire was sent by the same method.

rationales.A: Voluntary response bias applies when people select themselves into the sample; here the district chose whom to mail.
rationales.B: Families missing from the directory are left out of the sampling frame, so the sample is likely to differ from all parents.
rationales.C: Nonresponse concerns selected people who do not reply; the main problem here is that many parents were never selected at all.
rationales.D: A uniform method does not fix a frame that omits parents; the sample is still unrepresentative.

stem: A radio station asks listeners to call in during a morning show to vote on whether the city should build a new stadium, and it reports the percent of callers in favor. What is the most likely source of bias?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No bias, because a large number of listeners will call in.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Voluntary response bias, because only listeners with strong opinions are likely to call.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placebo effect, because the callers believe their vote matters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Confounding bias, because a lurking variable is mixed with the stadium vote.

rationales.A: A large number of responses does not make a self-selected group representative; the bias remains however many call.
rationales.B: Callers choose themselves, and people with strong feelings are more likely to respond, so the callers do not represent the city.
rationales.C: A placebo effect concerns responses to inactive treatments in experiments, not to opinion polls.
rationales.D: Confounding is a feature of comparing treatments or groups; this is a single poll of opinion.

stem: A city randomly selects 1,000 households from a complete list of all households and mails each a survey about recycling. Only 220 households return it. Which bias is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Undercoverage bias, because 780 households are missing from the data.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Response bias, because the survey asked about recycling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonresponse bias, because households that did not reply may differ from those that did.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Convenience sampling bias, because mailed surveys are the cheapest approach.

rationales.A: Those 780 were in the frame and were selected; they are missing due to not responding, not because they were excluded from the frame.
rationales.B: Response bias comes from untruthful or distorted answers, for example from wording; nothing in the setup points to that.
rationales.C: All households had a chance to be chosen, but 780 chosen households did not respond, and the 220 who replied may not represent them.
rationales.D: The households were chosen randomly from a complete list, so the selection was not by convenience.

stem: At a high school, a student is chosen at random. Let C be the event that the student is in a club and J the event that the student has a part-time job. P(C) = 0.50, P(J) = 0.20, and P(C and J) = 0.15. Are C and J independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because P(C and J) = 0.15 is not equal to P(C) + P(J) = 0.70.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, because P(C or J) = 0.55 is less than 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because P(C)P(J) = 0.10, which does not equal P(C and J) = 0.15.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because P(C and J) = 0.15 is smaller than both P(C) and P(J).

rationales.A: The addition of probabilities is not the independence check; the product is.
rationales.B: P(C or J) = 0.50 + 0.20 - 0.15 = 0.55 is a valid probability but says nothing about independence.
rationales.C: Independence requires P(C and J) = P(C)P(J); 0.50 x 0.20 = 0.10, but the joint probability is 0.15.
rationales.D: The joint probability is always at most each single probability; that does not test independence.

stem: At a school, P(a student rides the bus) = 0.50 and P(a student wears glasses) = 0.20. Among students who ride the bus, 20% wear glasses. Are riding the bus and wearing glasses independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, because P(glasses | bus) = 0.20 equals P(glasses) = 0.20.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because P(glasses | bus) = 0.20 is much smaller than P(bus) = 0.50.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because P(bus) + P(glasses) = 0.70, which is less than 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because both events can occur together, with P(bus and glasses) = 0.10 > 0.

rationales.A: If knowing a student rides the bus does not change the probability of wearing glasses, the events are independent.
rationales.B: This compares probabilities of different events; independence compares P(glasses | bus) with P(glasses).
rationales.C: A sum below 1 does not establish independence; the conditional probability equaling the marginal does.
rationales.D: Events that can occur together may still be independent; here 0.50 x 0.20 = 0.10 matches the joint probability.

stem: A cafe records 300 orders. Of these, 120 included coffee, 90 included a pastry, and 45 included both. For a randomly chosen order, are 'includes coffee' and 'includes a pastry' independent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, because 45 does not equal 120 + 90 = 210.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, because 120 + 90 = 210, which is less than the 300 orders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because the 45 orders with both are fewer than the 120 or the 90 orders with each item.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because P(coffee and pastry) = 45/300 = 0.15, which differs from P(coffee)P(pastry) = 0.40 x 0.30 = 0.12.

rationales.A: Independence is not tested by comparing the joint count to the sum of counts; the joint probability is compared with the product.
rationales.B: Whether the counts sum to less than the total says nothing about how the events relate.
rationales.C: A joint count is smaller than each single count for almost any two events, so this says nothing about independence; independence compares the joint probability with the product of the individual probabilities.
rationales.D: Independence needs the joint probability to equal the product of the individual probabilities; 0.15 is not 0.12.

stem: A student is chosen at random from a high school. Event S is that the student is a senior and event F is that the student is a freshman. Are S and F mutually exclusive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes, because being a senior and being a freshman are independent events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No, because P(S) + P(F) is less than 1.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No, because both groups belong to the same school.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, because a student cannot be both a senior and a freshman, so P(S and F) = 0.

rationales.A: Mutually exclusive events with nonzero probabilities are never independent, since knowing one occurred makes the other impossible.
rationales.B: Mutually exclusive events need not add to 1; other grades make the sum less than 1.
rationales.C: Belonging to the same school does not matter; what matters is whether the events can occur at the same time, and a student has only one grade.
rationales.D: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; one student has only one grade level.

stem: A student is chosen at random from a school. Event S is that the student plays on the soccer team and event O is that the student plays in the school orchestra. Are S and O mutually exclusive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No, but only if S and O are independent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Yes, because P(S and O) must equal P(S)P(O).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Yes, because soccer and orchestra are different activities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No, because a student can play on the soccer team and also play in the orchestra.

rationales.A: Whether they overlap does not depend on independence; the events can occur together in either case.
rationales.B: P(S and O) = P(S)P(O) is the independence condition, not a test for exclusive events, whose joint probability is 0.
rationales.C: Different activities do not prevent overlap; a student can do both, so P(S and O) can be greater than 0.
rationales.D: Events are mutually exclusive only if they cannot occur together; nothing prevents one student from doing both.

stem: A bag holds marbles of several colors. One marble is drawn at random. The probability it is red is 0.30 and the probability it is blue is 0.45. What is the probability that the marble is red or blue?

rationales.A: This is the difference 0.45 - 0.30 and does not represent the chance of either color.
rationales.B: This subtracts 0.135 as if red and blue could overlap, but a marble cannot be both, so nothing is subtracted.
rationales.C: This multiplies the probabilities (0.30 x 0.45), which would apply to independent events occurring together, not to 'or' for exclusive events.
rationales.D: A marble cannot be both red and blue, so the events are mutually exclusive and P(red or blue) = 0.30 + 0.45 = 0.75.

stem: A population of household incomes is strongly right-skewed. A statistician draws many random samples of size n = 2 and many of size n = 100, and plots the sample means from each. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The means from n = 100 will look approximately normal, but the means from n = 2 will still be noticeably right-skewed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The n = 2 means will look more normal than the n = 100 means, because small samples contain less skew.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both sets of sample means will look approximately normal, because every mean is an average.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither set will look normal, because a skewed population cannot give a normal sampling distribution.

rationales.A: The CLT needs a sufficiently large sample size; with n = 2 the sampling distribution retains much of the population's skew.
rationales.B: Normality of the sampling distribution improves as n increases, so n = 100 is much closer to normal.
rationales.C: Averaging alone is not enough; with a sample as small as 2 the shape stays close to the skewed population.
rationales.D: The CLT says that for a large enough n, the sampling distribution of means is approximately normal for nearly any population shape.

stem: Suppose 30% of all students at a university commute by bike. A random sample of n = 200 students is selected. What is the standard deviation (standard error) of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion of bike commuters?

rationales.A: The division by n belongs inside the square root; sqrt(0.21)/200 is about 0.0023.
rationales.B: This is the variance 0.00105; the square root was not taken.
rationales.D: This omits the factor (1 - p); sqrt(0.3/200) is about 0.039.

stem: In a large city, 55% of residents support a new park. A random sample of n = 150 residents is taken. Find the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion in favor.

stem: Two researchers test the same hypotheses about a population proportion using the same sample size and the same true proportion. Researcher 1 uses a significance level of alpha = 0.10 and Researcher 2 uses alpha = 0.01. Which test has greater power?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Researcher 2's test, because a lower Type I error rate also means a lower Type II error rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Researcher 1's test, because a larger alpha makes rejecting the null hypothesis easier when it is false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They have equal power, because both use the same hypotheses and sample size.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Researcher 2's test, because a smaller alpha requires stronger evidence.

rationales.A: Lowering alpha raises the chance of a Type II error, so power falls.
rationales.B: Increasing alpha enlarges the rejection region, which raises the probability of rejecting a false null, so power is higher.
rationales.C: Power also depends on alpha; changing it changes the rejection region and therefore the power.
rationales.D: Demanding stronger evidence makes it harder to reject, which lowers power.

stem: Two tests of H0: p = 0.50 vs Ha: p > 0.50 use the same sample size and significance level. In one situation the true proportion is 0.55, and in the other the true proportion is 0.70. Which situation gives the test greater power?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They have the same power, because the sample size and alpha are the same.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The situation with true p = 0.55, because it is closer to the null value.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The situation with true p = 0.70, because a larger gap from the null value makes a false null easier to detect.

rationales.A: Power also depends on how far the true value is from the null, so these two situations differ.
rationales.B: A smaller gap is harder to detect, which lowers power.
rationales.C: The farther the true parameter lies from the hypothesized value, the greater the probability of rejecting H0.
rationales.D: Power is the probability of rejecting a false null (1 minus Type II error), not alpha.

stem: A school district tests H0: a new tutoring program does not change mean reading scores against Ha: the program raises mean reading scores. In this setting, what does the power of the test measure for a particular size of improvement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The chance the test rejects H0 when the program has no effect on scores.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The chance the test rejects H0 when the program truly raises scores by that amount.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The chance that the program truly raises reading scores, given the data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chance the test fails to reject H0 when the program truly raises scores.

rationales.A: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error, and its probability is alpha, not power.
rationales.B: Power is the probability that the test correctly rejects the null hypothesis when the alternative is true for a specific effect size; it equals 1 minus beta.
rationales.C: Power is a probability about the test's decision for a given true effect, not the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
rationales.D: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a Type II error with probability beta; power is 1 minus beta.

stem: A test of whether a new bus route changes the proportion of on-time arrivals gives p = 0.03 with alpha = 0.05. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reject H0, which proves the alternative hypothesis is true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fail to reject H0, because 0.03 is smaller than 0.05 and so the evidence is too weak.

choices.label: D

rationales.A: Because p = 0.03 is less than alpha = 0.05, the result is statistically significant and the data provide convincing evidence for Ha.
rationales.B: A test gives evidence, not proof; the conclusion should use language such as convincing evidence.
rationales.C: A p-value smaller than alpha is evidence against H0; it leads to rejection, not failure to reject.
rationales.D: The p-value is computed assuming H0 is true; it is not the probability that H0 is true.

stem: A hospital tests whether a new protocol reduces readmission rates and uses alpha = 0.01. The test gives p = 0.047. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reject H0, since p = 0.047 is below the common 0.05 cutoff.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fail to reject H0, which means H0 is true with probability 1 - 0.047 = 0.953.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fail to reject H0; there is not convincing evidence at the 0.01 level.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reject H0, since 0.047 is close to 0.01.

rationales.A: The cutoff for this test is alpha = 0.01, set in advance, not 0.05.
rationales.B: The p-value does not give the probability that H0 is true, and failing to reject does not prove it.
rationales.C: Because p = 0.047 is greater than alpha = 0.01, the evidence is not strong enough at this level.
rationales.D: Being close to alpha does not justify rejection; the rule is to reject only if p is less than alpha.
